mechanism_claim: With three fixed capital slots, a weak third candidate should usually be assigned capacity 0 rather than mechanically filling the third slot. Capacity 1 represents a concentrated bet on a single high-conviction candidate, capacity 2 trades one unit of concentration for diversification, and capacity 3 should be reserved for a third candidate whose point-in-time quality is comparable to the first two. A weak candidate is characterized by low 20-day up-day participation, subdued near-term volume expansion, weak 20-day momentum, and proximity to the 20- and 50-day moving averages. Adding that candidate can reduce average quality and increase the chance that an apparently valid breakout fails or produces ruin, while 0 and sometimes 1 preserve optionality for future candidates. This claim concerns the incremental information carried by the third-ranked candidate, not ticker identity or calendar effects.
evidence_for: The archaeology identifies eight false-positive-ruin cases and one case carrying both false-positive-ruin and selected-winner labels; these show that breakout-like observations can be selected at entry and subsequently fail.

Several selected-winner cases have weak-looking point-in-time features, so observable weakness is not proof of future failure. For example, entity_2f86543bf6 had mom_20 near zero, slightly negative ma20_slope_5, and small px_vs_ma20, yet its later bucket was large_win. This supports abstention as a risk-control hypothesis but also argues for uncertainty rather than a deterministic cutoff.

Relative to selected winners, false negatives have materially lower median up_day_ratio_20 (0.500 versus 0.625), vol_ratio_5_20 (1.179 versus 1.424), mom_20 (0.058 versus 0.163), and px_vs_ma50 (0.056 versus 0.127). The adaptive rule should therefore treat a weak third candidate as low-priority, not as a claim that the candidate will necessarily lose.

The false-positive-ruin examples often show moderate entry extension without uniformly stronger breadth, volume, or momentum. For example, entity_84824e6a20 had ibd_entry_close_vs_trigger_pct 0.0738, up_day_ratio_20 0.40, mom_20 0.067, and a later ruin bucket. This pattern is consistent with a low-quality third slot diluting the portfolio's stronger signals.

The archaeological label method itself uses future W4 performance, so selected_winner, false-positive-ruin, false-negative-relative, and false-negative-big-winner are outcome labels and must not be used as if available at the decision date. The falsification test must use only entry-time candidate features and known portfolio state.
evidence_against: Weak point-in-time features are not sufficient to justify capacity 0. Entity_2f86543bf6 was weak on up_day_ratio_20 and momentum yet later classified as a large winner, while entity_3adc078f01 had modest up-day participation and volume ratio but later a large winner bucket.

The supplied evidence contains no simultaneous, matched observations of the same candidate under capacities 0, 1, 2, and 3. It therefore cannot identify the causal effect of changing capacity or establish that capacity 0 dominates capacity 1 or 2.

The 27-case sample is small, discovery-train-only, and includes only a limited number of explicit false-negative and false-positive cases. It cannot support a stable numerical threshold, guarantee monotonic returns, or establish that weak candidates should be excluded in all market states.

The evidence does not provide the complete ranking distribution, cross-sectional candidate universe, contemporaneous competing candidates, or the later performance of all alternatives. Consequently, a weak third candidate may be inferior to the held candidates but still superior to leaving capital uninvested or to a future replacement.
Outcome labels include future W4 returns and relative comparisons, so using their patterns to define a present-time policy risks lookahead bias and outcome-based selection.
falsifiable_predictions: For third-ranked candidates below prespecified thresholds for up_day_ratio_20, vol_ratio_5_20, mom_20, and distance above ma20 and ma50, the observed next-period performance distribution should be shifted toward lower returns and higher loss frequency than for third-ranked candidates above the thresholds. A failure of this ordering would falsify the proposed weak-candidate abstention mechanism.

Within the weak-third stratum, a policy that leaves the slot open should outperform a policy that always allocates the third slot on mean return per unit risk, and should avoid the largest observed ruin outcomes. The comparison must use identical dates, candidate universe, transaction costs, and capital sizing.

Conditional on a weak third candidate, capacity 1 should be chosen when the first candidate has substantially stronger point-in-time breadth, momentum, volume confirmation, and moving-average separation than the second and third candidates. Capacity 1 should deliver lower drawdown or better return concentration than capacity 2 or 3, while accepting lower diversification.

Capacity 2 should dominate capacity 3 when the second candidate is materially stronger than the third on the same entry-time quality features. If adding the third slot does not improve return per unit risk, this would falsify the proposed diversification benefit and support abstention.

Capacity 3 should only be selected when the third candidate is close to the first two on quality and its incremental entry evidence is strong. In such a high-quality third-candidate stratum, capacity 3 should not produce significantly worse risk-adjusted performance than capacity 2, after controlling for transaction costs.

The adaptive rule is falsified if, after controlling for candidate quality and contemporaneous portfolio composition, capacity has no relationship with incremental next-period return, loss probability, or drawdown, or if the estimated value of the third slot is the same for weak and strong third candidates.

The mechanism is also falsified by a reproducible exception: weak third candidates whose point-in-time breadth, volume, and momentum are weak but whose subsequent return consistently exceeds the corresponding strong-third-candidate group after costs. Such a result would indicate that the proposed quality dimensions are mis-specified or temporally unstable.
policy_implications: Do not fill all three slots solely because a candidate satisfies a generic breakout trigger. Use capacity as a ranked, testable decision variable: 0 for a clearly weak third candidate, 1 for one dominant setup, 2 for two comparably strong setups, and 3 only for three similarly strong setups.

Estimate capacity effects with a fully entry-time-defined policy and causal or quasi-causal comparisons. Use date-level blocking, matched candidate ranks, and identical capital scaling; do not evaluate capacity using outcome labels as input features.

Use calibration and walk-forward validation to set thresholds for weak versus strong candidates. Avoid embedding the observed false-positive and false-negative labels directly in the rule, because those labels depend on future returns.

Interpret capacity 0 as preserving capital and avoiding dilution, not as a prediction of an immediate market decline. A weak third candidate can still win, so the policy objective should emphasize incremental risk-adjusted portfolio value and the opportunity cost of not holding a replacement.

The current evidence is insufficient to implement a definitive capacity assignment. The appropriate conclusion is UNRESOLVED pending a matched entry-time experiment capable of separating candidate-selection quality from the portfolio-construction effect of adding one, two, or three positions.
